newsitem.title: FRANCE: ATHLETICS-GEBRSELASSIE GIVES HINT OF THINGS TO COME.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-GEBRSELASSIE GIVES HINT OF THINGS TO COME.

text.p: On the track Haile Gebrselassie confirmed at the weekend that he remains the world's premier distance runnner.
Off track, he gave a hint of things to come in the rapidly changing world of athletics.

Gebrselassie romped home in the men's 3,000 metres on the final day of the sixth world championships on Sunday, winning $50,000 at the first International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) championship to offer prize money.
On the previous day Gebrselassie held a joint news conference with Noureddine Morceli to announce a winner-take-all clash over two miles in Hengelo on May 31.
The pair, Olympic champions respectively over 10,000 metres and 1,500, will be racing for a purse of $1 million.

They have clearly agreed that two miles will be a fair test for a long distance and middle-distance runner. Morceli has expressed ambitions to extend his range to 5,000 metres and Gebrselassie has competed with distinction over 1,500 indoors.
The following day another pair of Olympic champions, Michael Johnson and Donovan Bailey, will stage a $1 million challenge over 150 metres in Toronto.
This distance too is a compromise designed to provide the fairest test for the Atlanta 200 and 100 gold medallists.
It is difficult to see what either race will prove and uncertain yet how much television or spectator interest they will generate.
But they represent the next stage in the IAAF's continuing battle to promote the sport in a fiercely competitive market.
Senior members of the federation believe head-to-head clashes are the way for the sport to advance.
They say the continuing pressure for world records on the grand prix circuit will be ultimately self-defeating, providing overwhelming temptation for athletes to take drugs.
The Toronto organisers plan to stage other duels with Sergei Bubka takng on Okkert Brits in the pole vault and veterans Jackie Joyner-Kersee and Heike Drechsler clashing in the long jump.
The three-day meeting here pointed the way to an exciting outdoor season which will culminate in the Athens world championships.

Kenyan-born Dane Wilson Kipketer broke the world 800 metres record twice and can now look forward confidently to breaking Sebastian Coe's outdoor mark set in 1981, the oldest track record on the books.
Hicham el Guerrouj, who fell in the Olympic final last year, retained the indoor 1,500 metres title and has the potential to take Morceli's outdoor title away from the Algerian.
Prize money for medal winners and bonuses for world records succeeded in attracting a number of athletes who would not otherwise have bothered to come to Paris.
The future of the championships is assured, if only as a shop window for the sport in the northern off-season.
And as a further sign of the times, there was a significant addition to the results lists circulated among the media.
As well as their country, all competitors now have their shoe brand printed on the results.
